planting.note: Plant corms shallowly in autumn in mild-winter regions or in spring elsewhere, after danger of hard frost has passed.

directions: Plant corms in free-draining, sandy soil where summers stay on the dry side, since this Western Cape species rots quickly in heavy or waterlogged ground. Wiry, wand-like stems carry a one-sided spray of small, flattened orange-red flowers with a distinctive notched, hatchet-shaped tepal in late winter to spring. Where winters drop much below 20°F, lift and store corms dry over the cold season or grow in pots that can be moved under cover. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally before withholding water for the dormant season.
sources: Manning, Goldblatt & Snijman, Bulbs of South Africa

planting.note: Plant corms in autumn where winters are mild and dry summer dormancy can be provided; otherwise start in spring after frost.

directions: Give this small winter-rainfall-region species sharply drained, gritty soil and keep it bone dry through its summer dormancy to prevent corm rot. Orange flowers marked with a dark, scorched-looking blotch at the base of each tepal open on short, slender spikes in spring, giving the species its common name. It suits a rock garden or bulb frame where a dry summer rest can be guaranteed, and is best grown in pots in climates with wet summers. Divide offset corms when dormant and replant promptly to avoid desiccation.
sources: Manning, Goldblatt & Snijman, Bulbs of South Africa

planting.note: Mount on a slab or pot in a fine bark-and-sphagnum mix when actively growing.

directions: Mount this miniature Madagascan species on a cork or fern slab, or pot it in a small clay pot with a fine, fast-draining bark mix, since its compact fan of leaves resents being buried too deeply. Fragrant, star-shaped white flowers with a long nectar spur open singly or in twos from the leaf axils and are strongly scented at night, a trait shared with its larger relative A. sesquipedale. Keep humidity high and water year-round, easing back only slightly in winter, and provide bright, filtered light rather than direct sun to avoid scorching the thin leaves.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — World Checklist of Selected Plant Families

planting.note: Mount on a slab or pot in a coarse, fast-draining orchid mix when actively growing.

directions: Grow this tough, drought-tolerant species from Madagascar and the Comoros mounted on a slab or in a shallow basket, since its thick, succulent, distichous leaves store water and are prone to rot if kept constantly soggy. Waxy white, star-shaped flowers with a fragrant night scent are borne a few at a time from the leaf axils over an extended winter-to-spring season. It tolerates brighter light and drier conditions between waterings than most angraecoids, making it a forgiving choice for a sunny windowsill or bright greenhouse bench.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — World Checklist of Selected Plant Families

planting.note: Divide and plant rooted sections of rhizome in spring once the ground is workable.

directions: Selected at Spetchley Park Gardens, this plume poppy cultivar bears airy, coral-pink-flushed plumes above the same deeply lobed, glaucous blue-green foliage typical of the species, standing well above most summer perennials. Give it room to run, as the rhizomes spread steadily in loose, fertile soil, and site it at the back of a border or in a bed where its colonizing habit is welcome. Cut stems release an orange latex sap that can irritate skin, so handle with gloves when dividing or deadheading. Shelter from strong wind or stake in exposed sites, since the tall flowering stems can lean once plumes are fully open.

planting.note: Divide and pot in a coarse bark mix in spring as new growth begins.

directions: Pot this large-flowered Ecuadorian and Peruvian cloud-forest species in a coarse, open bark mix that drains quickly while still holding some moisture around the roots. Each flower is strikingly large for the genus, with creamy white to pale yellow tepals heavily blotched in deep maroon-red around a contrasting white and yellow lip, borne singly from the base of the clustered pseudobulbs. Cooler night temperatures and consistently high humidity encourage the best bloom, so an intermediate greenhouse or bright, humid windowsill with good air movement suits it better than a hot, dry room. Repot only when the mix breaks down or the plant outgrows its container, since Maxillaria resents frequent disturbance.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — World Checklist of Selected Plant Families
